    The other side can walk away at your cost

    The supplier can quit the contract with 60 days' notice whenever it likes — but you've already paid big fees upfront, and nothing in the contract says you get that money back. They could walk away with your cash and you'd have no refund right.

  • ⋯

    Under clause 7.3: "The Supplier may terminate this Agreement for convenience by giving the Bank not less than 60 days' notice.", the Supplier may end the contract.

    What this meansPlain English

    The supplier can quit the contract with 60 days' notice whenever it likes — but you've already paid big fees upfront, and nothing in the contract says you get that money back. They could walk away with your cash and you'd have no refund right.

    Why this severity
    • Eastgate Savings Bank (the Bank): the core of the deal
    • Nothing to recover
    • One party can bring it about alone
    • A lawyer's view: a real problem
    How it can play out
    1. 1Step 1The Bank keeps to the contract: it does everything the contract asks of it - clauses a, b, c, 4.1, 4.3, 4.5, 4.6, 8.4 among it.
    2. 2Step 2

      The Supplier then ends the contract under , by its own choice

      The Supplier may terminate this Agreement for convenience by giving the Bank not less than 60 days' notice.

    3. 3Outcome
      • The Supplier walks away at will
      • The Bank loses money the Bank paid in advance for a period or a service it will now not receive and nothing gives it back
      • Clause 7.4 says it is kept

  • High
    A reference to a clause that does not exist

    The contract points to a rule that doesn't exist — it references a clause that was never written. So whatever it's trying to say there is effectively meaningless.

  • High Both sides
    A term left to be agreed and never fixed

    The price for year two isn't set — the contract just says you'll 'agree it later'. If you can't agree, there's no fallback, so the supplier could hold you hostage on price.

  • High Both sides
    Two clauses give the same thing to different owners

    Two clauses say opposite things about who owns the work product: one says you own it once you pay, the other says the supplier keeps it and only lends you limited use. Ownership is left in doubt.

  • Medium
    A table does not add up

    The fee table's numbers don't match its own total: the items add up to £20,000 but the contract says £25,000. Someone could demand the higher figure.

  • Medium Hurts Bank
    A term used but never defined

    The contract uses the word 'Licensor' as if it names a specific party, but never says who that is. Obligations tied to that word are unenforceable because nobody knows who it means.

  • Low Not confident Both sides
    No consequence for a confidentiality breach

    The contract requires confidentiality but says nothing about what happens if someone leaks your secrets — no penalty, no compensation, no right to exit. A breach would cost you real money with no contractual remedy.

  • Low Not confident Both sides
    Silent on a change of control

    If the supplier is bought by another company, the contract says nothing about what happens. A new, unknown owner could inherit (or ignore) the deal with no say from you.

  • Low Not confident
    No roles set for personal data

    The contract is silent on who handles personal data and in what legal role. That's a compliance gap — if data is mishandled, responsibility is unclear and you could both be exposed.
